Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$

These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

derivations.claim: Put $g_R=g\mathbf1_{B(0,R)}$. By [F3], $$\|g-g_R\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{|\xi|>R}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2d\xi\longrightarrow0\qquad(R\to\infty).$$ Choose $R$ so this norm is less than a prescribed $\varepsilon/2$.

Let $f$ be any Schwartz function and define $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$. Polynomial multiples of derivatives of $f$ have arbitrarily rapid decay by [F5], so they and their derivatives are integrable, including on each coordinate line with the other coordinates fixed. Differentiation in $\xi$ is justified by dominated convergence [F6] using these integrable moments. Apply [F7] on each coordinate line to such a function and its Fourier exponential: the derivative products are integrable and the boundary product tends to zero. Absolute Fubini [F6] then combines the coordinate identities and shows that every $\xi^\gamma D_\xi^\alpha\widehat f(\xi)$ is a finite linear combination of Fourier transforms of derivatives of polynomial multiples of $f$. Each such function is in $L^1$ by [F5], so its Fourier transform is bounded; hence $\widehat f$ is Schwartz and in $L^1$. In particular $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi<\infty$, by polar integration [F6].

On the bounded ball $O=B(0,R+1)$, the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ is bounded above by a finite constant $C_R$. The restriction of $g_R$ to $O$ lies in $L^2(O)$, so [F2] gives $\phi\in C_c^\infty(O)$ with $\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}<\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{C_R})$. Extending $\phi$ by zero is still smooth and compactly supported on $\mathbb R^d$ because its support is compactly contained in $O$, and $$\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2_s}^2\le C_R\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}^2<\varepsilon^2/4.$$

For $\epsilon>0$, absolute Fubini [F6] and the Gaussian transform [F6] give $$\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}e^{-\pi\epsilon|\xi|^2}d\xi=\int f(y)\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|x-y|^2/\epsilon}dy=(f*G_\epsilon)(x),$$ where $G_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|z|^2/\epsilon}$. Since $\widehat f\in L^1$, dominated convergence sends the left side to $\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}d\xi$. The right side tends to $f(x)$: given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity at $x$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x-z)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $|z|<\delta$. Since $G_\epsilon$ has total mass one, the contribution from this ball is at most $\varepsilon$; boundedness of $f$ and the Gaussian tail estimate from scaling make the contribution on $|z|\ge\delta$ tend to zero. Thus Fourier inversion holds and $f=U_{\widehat f}\in H^s$.

For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, differentiation under the integral is justified by the compactly supported integrable moments. For each coordinate, apply [F7] with the smooth compactly supported factor $(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\phi(\xi)$ (or a derivative of it) and the inverse Fourier exponential; both derivative products are integrable and the boundary product is zero outside a bounded interval. Repetition and absolute Fubini [F6] give $$x^\beta D_x^\alpha U_\phi(x)=(-1)^{|\beta|}(2\pi i)^{-|\beta|}\int \partial_\xi^\beta\big((2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\phi(\xi)\big)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}d\xi.$$ The right side is uniformly bounded by the $L^1$ norm of a smooth compactly supported function. Hence every Schwartz seminorm of $U_\phi$ is finite, so $U_\phi$ is Schwartz.

([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$

symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.

isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

For every real $p$,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k^p}\text{ converges}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F5] choose a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $\overline B(0,1/2)$ and supported in $B(0,1)$. Set $\eta(\xi)=(\rho(\xi)+\rho(-\xi))/2$. Then $\eta$ is smooth, even, nonnegative, at most one, still equals one on the half-radius ball, and is supported in the unit ball. Define $\psi(z)=\int\eta(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}d\xi$. Reflection invariance of Lebesgue measure [F3] and Euler's formula [F9] make $\psi$ real and even, and monotonicity [F7] gives $\psi(0)=\int\eta\ge\lambda(B(0,1/2))>0$.

Since $\eta$ is smooth and compactly supported, it is Schwartz by [F8], so $\widehat\eta$ is Schwartz and $\psi(z)=\widehat\eta(-z)$ is Schwartz as well. For $|z|\ge1$, choose a coordinate $j$ with $|z_j|\ge|z|/\sqrt d$; the Schwartz seminorm $\sup_\xi|\xi_j^M\widehat\eta(\xi)|<\infty$ gives $|\psi(z)|\le C_M|z|^{-M}$. For $|z|\le1$, [F7] and $|e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}|=1$ from [F9] give $|\psi(z)|\le\int\eta$. Combining the two bounds yields $|\psi(z)|\le C'_M(1+|z|)^{-M}$.

Fix $i$. The open balls $B(x_j,q)$ are pairwise disjoint because center distances are at least $2q$. If $n\le|x_i-x_j|/q<n+1$, then $B(x_j,q)\subset B(x_i,(n+2)q)$. Translation invariance and dilation change of variables in [F3] give $\lambda(B(x,r))=r^d\lambda(B(0,1))$; this unit-ball measure is finite and positive. Finite additivity on the disjoint balls therefore bounds the number of such $j$ by $(n+2)^d$. Hence, for any integer $M>d+1$ and $T\ge1$, [step 2.1] yields the uniform row-sum estimate $$\sum_{j\ne i}\left|\psi\!\left(T(x_i-x_j)/q\right)\right|\le C_MT^{-M}\sum_{n\ge1}(n+2)^dn^{-M}.$$ For $n\ge1$, $(n+2)^d\le3^dn^d$, so this series is bounded by $3^d\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-(M-d)}$, which converges by [F11] because $M-d>1$. Choose one fixed $T$ large enough that this upper bound is at most $\psi(0)/2$.

For any $c\in\mathbb C^N$, the quadratic form of $H_{ij}=\psi(T(x_i-x_j)/q)$ satisfies $$c^*Hc\ge\left(\psi(0)-\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}|H_{ij}|\right)\|c\|_2^2\ge\frac{\psi(0)}2\|c\|_2^2,$$ because each off-diagonal pair is bounded using $2|c_i||c_j|\le|c_i|^2+|c_j|^2$. By the change of variables $\zeta=(q/T)\xi$, $$\int_{|\xi|\le T/q}\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi\ge\int\eta(q\xi/T)\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi=(T/q)^d c^*Hc.$$ The first inequality uses $0\le\eta\le1$ and support in the unit ball.

On $|\xi|\le T/q$ and $q\le1$, set $B=(a^2+4\pi^2T^2)q^{-2}$. Then $a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2\le a^2+4\pi^2T^2/q^2\le B$. Monotonicity and the power laws [F10] give $$w(\xi)\ge A B^{-s}=A\left(a^2+4\pi^2T^2\right)^{-s}q^{2s}.$$ Using the Fourier quadratic-form identity from [F1] and step 4.1 gives $c^*K_Xc\ge c_0q^{2s-d}\|c\|_2^2=c_0q^{2\nu}\|c\|_2^2$ for a constant $c_0>0$ independent of $X,q,N$. Thus [F4] yields $\lambda_{\min}(K_X)\ge c_0q^{2\nu}$.

By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis and write $K_X=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. If $Q=(q_{ij})$, then $$\operatorname{tr}(K_X)=\sum_i(K_X)_{ii}=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j=N,$$ since each column of $Q$ has unit norm and [F2] gives diagonal entries $k(0)=1$. By step 5.1 all eigenvalues are positive, so $\lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N$. In this eigenbasis the induced 2-norms of $K_X$ and $K_X^{-1}$ are $\lambda_{\max}$ and $1/\lambda_{\min}$, respectively, by [F6]. The definition $\kappa_2(K_X)=\|K_X\|_2\|K_X^{-1}\|_2$ therefore gives $\kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2\nu}$. The $N=1$ case follows directly from $k(0)=1$ and the same definition.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let either $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with
$p\ge 1$ or $p=\infty$, and let
$A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an invertible real matrix
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), so that the linear system
$Ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=A^{-1}b$ for every right-hand side
$b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **condition number of the linear system** (equivalently,
of the matrix $A$) with respect to the induced $p$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], using its separately defined infinity case when
$p=\infty$, is

$$\kappa_p(A)\;:=\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p\;\in\;[1,+\infty).$$

**The value is at least one and is never infinite.** The inverse $A^{-1}$ is the
unique two-sided inverse of $A$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]),
so $AA^{-1}=I_n$ and $A^{-1}A=I_n$. For rational finite $p$,
submultiplicativity and normalisation are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]].
For $p=\infty$, the same properties follow directly from the defining
supremum: $\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\lVert A\rVert_\infty\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
and applying this estimate twice gives submultiplicativity, while
$I_nx=x$ gives $\lVert I_n\rVert_\infty=1$. Hence in either case

$$1=\lVert I_n\rVert_p=\lVert AA^{-1}\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p=\kappa_p(A).$$

Equivalently, $\kappa_p(A)$ is the product of the largest factor by which $A$
stretches a nonzero vector and the largest factor by which $A^{-1}$ stretches
one. Applying the same estimate to $A^{-1}$ in place of $A$ gives
$\kappa_p(A^{-1})=\kappa_p(A)$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: The cube is bounded and Lipschitz. At a boundary point $p$, let $I$ be the nonempty set of active coordinates ($p_j=0$ or $1$), with inward signs $\sigma_j=1$ at $0$ and $-1$ at $1$. Put $u_j=\sigma_j/\sqrt{|I|}$ for $j\in I$ and $u_j=0$ otherwise. In the orthogonal coordinates $x=p+y+tu$ with $y\perp u$, a sufficiently small neighborhood has no constraints from inactive coordinates, and the active inequalities reduce to $$t>\max_{j\in I}(-\sqrt{|I|}\,\sigma_j y_j).$$ This is the epigraph of a finite maximum of linear functions, hence a local Lipschitz graph with the cube on one side. The cube also satisfies the uniform cone condition. For $x\in[0,1]^d$, choose signs $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ take $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$ for each coordinate. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$.

Distinct midpoint sites have fill distance at most $\sqrt d/(2m)$. Since $m$ is odd, $x_0\in X_m$. By continuity in [F2], choose $\epsilon_m>0$ so that $|1-k(\delta e_1)|<1/m$ whenever $0<\delta<\epsilon_m$, then choose $0<\delta_m<\min\{\epsilon_m,1/(4m^2)\}$. Strict positive definiteness for $x_0$ and $x_0+\delta_me_1$ makes $1-k(\delta_me_1)>0$, so $0<1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. Put $Z_m=X_m\cup\{x_0+\delta_me_1\}$. The new site is inside the cube because $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/2$. Every other grid site is at distance at least $1/m$ from $x_0$, while $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/(2m)$, so the new site is distinct from all grid sites. At the boundary corner $0$, the nearest grid point is $\left(1/(2m),\ldots,1/(2m)\right)$, at distance $\sqrt d/(2m)$; the new site has squared distance $d/4+\delta_m+\delta_m^2>d/(4m^2)$, so $\min_{z\in Z_m}|z|=\sqrt d/(2m)$. For $D_m(x)=\min_{z\in Z_m}|x-z|$, the triangle inequality gives $|D_m(x)-D_m(y)|\le|x-y|$. Since $x_n=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)\in\Omega$ for $n\ge2$ and $x_n\to0$, $D_m(x_n)\to D_m(0)$; the fill-distance supremum therefore satisfies $h_{Z_m}\ge\sqrt d/(2m)\ge1/(2m)$. Adding a site cannot increase fill distance, so also $h_{Z_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$. The separation radius satisfies $0<q_{Z_m}\le\delta_m/2<1/(8m^2)$; consequently $\rho_{Z_m}=h_{Z_m}/q_{Z_m}>4m\to\infty$.

Let $u$ be the unit vector with entries $1/\sqrt2$ and $-1/\sqrt2$ at the new site and $x_0$, and zero elsewhere. The corresponding Rayleigh quotient is $$u^{\mathsf T}K_{Z_m}u=\tfrac12(1+1-2k(\delta_me_1))=1-k(\delta_me_1).$$ Hence [F3] gives $0<\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})\le1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. By [F3] choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $Q$ and write $K_{Z_m}=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. Since every diagonal entry is $1$, $$\operatorname{tr}K_{Z_m}=|Z_m|=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j,$$ so $\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})$ is at least the average eigenvalue, namely $1$. For a unit vector $v=Qc$, orthogonality gives $\|K_{Z_m}v\|_2^2=\sum_j\lambda_j^2c_j^2\le\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})^2$, with equality at a top eigenvector; the same calculation for $K_{Z_m}^{-1}$ gives induced 2-norm $1/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})$. Thus [F4] gives $\kappa_2(K_{Z_m})=\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})>m$. Together with step 1.2, this gives $h_{Z_m}\to0$, $\rho_{Z_m}\to\infty$, and condition number tending to infinity.
